## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where users configuring FAL provider request policy for media generation would not have that policy applied to FAL image generation HTTP requests.

FAL HTTP config now passes `models.providers.fal.request` into the existing provider HTTP request-policy resolver. This keeps FAL on the shared provider request seam and does not change model parameters, generation parsing, or media download behavior.

FAL media generation requests can now honor configured request headers, proxy, TLS, and private-network policy through the existing provider request policy mechanism.

target.title: fix(msteams): reset sessions on app removal lifecycle
target.body:
Closes #99054

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where Microsoft Teams users who remove a personal app/bot and later add it again can continue the same OpenClaw server-side DM session, allowing the bot to use prior conversation context after an app lifecycle boundary.

This targets Teams app-management lifecycle signals that the bot can actually observe. Live capture showed Teams' local "Remove chat history" action can arrive later as an ordinary message in the same personal `conversation.id`, with no `installationUpdate`, `conversationUpdate`, `membersAdded`, or `membersRemoved` activity. This PR does not claim to detect that fully local clear-chat action when Teams gives the bot no lifecycle or conversation-boundary signal.

## Why This Change Was Made

Teams now routes `installationUpdate` removal activities and bot `membersRemoved` conversation updates into a lifecycle handler. On a removal boundary, the handler removes the cached Teams conversation reference, rotates the matching OpenClaw session entry to a new session id with `updatedAt: 0`, and clears provider-owned route/delivery/origin metadata so the next inbound message cannot resume the removed chat transcript.

The handler also treats a personal `installationUpdate action=add` as a reinstall boundary only when an existing route-matched Teams DM session is already active. That catches tenants or flows where the re-add signal is visible but the prior remove signal was missed, without resetting first-time installs. Finally, inbound personal DMs check for a stored same-user/same-bot conversation reference with a different Teams `conversation.id`; when Teams exposes that boundary, OpenClaw removes the previous reference and rotates the DM session.

## User Impact

After a true Teams app removal and re-add, the next inbound message starts from a fresh OpenClaw session instead of silently resuming prior DM or channel context. Operators also avoid retaining a cached proactive-send reference for the removed Teams conversation.

For Teams clear-chat/reopen flows, the patch protects the observable case where Teams gives the bot a new personal conversation id. If Teams reuses the same server-side conversation id and sends no lifecycle event, there is no bot-visible signal in the captured payloads; that remains a Teams platform limitation rather than a claim made by this PR.

Existing welcome-card behavior, normal messages, reactions, and unrelated lifecycle events are unchanged.

## Evidence

- Live corrected Dale smoke:
  - Baseline before app removal used a synthetic marker.
  - Teams app removal emitted `installationUpdate action=remove`.
  - Handler logged `msteams lifecycle remove handled`, `reason=installation-remove`, `conversationType=personal`, `conversationRemoved=true`, `sessionsReset=1`.
  - The session entry rotated to a new redacted session id with `updatedAt: 0` and no Teams route/delivery/origin metadata.
  - After re-add, Teams showed the welcome card and the verification prompt used a fresh session; the bot did not recall the pre-removal marker.
- Live Teams `Remove chat history` follow-up after deploying this branch:
  - Sent a synthetic pre-clear marker.
  - Used Teams `Remove chat history`, opened the app/chat again, and sent a verification prompt.
  - No `installationUpdate add`, lifecycle/remove activity, or DM conversation-boundary handler log appeared.
  - The same OpenClaw session id remained active, and the bot could recall the pre-clear marker.
  - This confirms the PR should not claim to fix Teams local clear-history behavior when Teams sends no lifecycle event and reuses the same server-side conversation id.
- Added regression coverage for:
  - personal `installationUpdate/remove`
  - personal `installationUpdate/remove-upgrade`
  - first-install `installationUpdate/add` with no active session
  - personal `installationUpdate/add` when an existing session is active
  - ignored channel `installationUpdate/add`
  - channel bot `membersRemoved`
  - ignored non-bot `membersRemoved`
  - race-safe session rotation
  - personal DM conversation-id boundary rotation
  - no rotation for matching personal conversation ids
  - no rotation for different stored bot ids
- Added monitor-level coverage proving the Teams activity shim dispatches `installationUpdate` and `membersRemoved` activities to registered lifecycle handlers.
- Validation:
  - `pnpm test extensions/msteams/src/monitor-handler/lifecycle-handler.test.ts` - 11 tests passed.
  - `pnpm test extensions/msteams/src/monitor-handler/message-handler.authz.test.ts` - 18 tests passed.
  - `pnpm test extensions/msteams` - 71 files passed, 1007 tests passed.
  - `pnpm run lint:extensions:bundled` - passed.
  - `pnpm format:check extensions/msteams/src/monitor-handler/lifecycle-handler.ts extensions/msteams/src/monitor-handler/lifecycle-handler.test.ts extensions/msteams/src/monitor-handler/message-handler.ts` - passed.
  - `git diff --check` - passed.



---

Migration note: This PR replaces #100371 with the same published head commit, moved from `spinen/openclaw` to `jimmypuckett/openclaw` so OpenClaw maintainers and repository automation can update the contribution without transferring authorship. Prior review, proof, and CI history remain available on #100371.

target.title: fix(msteams): add timeouts to file consent upload requests
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Teams file consent uploads validated the SharePoint consent URL, then performed the upload PUT without a request deadline. If the upload request never completed, the accepted file delivery path could remain pending indefinitely.

## Why This Change Was Made

Add a bounded consent upload timeout using the existing timer timeout resolver, and keep the abort timer active until the upload request finishes. The upload deadline is transfer-aware: it keeps a 5 minute base stall bound, then adds size-derived transfer budget so valid large SharePoint uploads are not cut off by a fixed 5 minute ceiling. The SSRF host/IP validation and upload headers/body semantics are unchanged.

## User Impact

When a Teams file consent upload stalls, OpenClaw now aborts the request instead of waiting forever, so the file delivery flow can fail quickly and surface the error path. Large valid file-consent uploads get additional budget based on payload size instead of sharing the same fixed deadline as a small upload.

## Evidence

- `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs extensions/msteams/src/file-consent.test.ts extensions/msteams/src/request-timeout.test.ts` passed: 68 tests.
- `node_modules/.bin/oxfmt --check extensions/msteams/src/request-timeout.ts extensions/msteams/src/file-consent.ts extensions/msteams/src/file-consent.test.ts extensions/msteams/src/request-timeout.test.ts` passed.
- `node_modules/.bin/oxlint --tsconfig config/tsconfig/oxlint.extensions.json extensions/msteams/src/request-timeout.ts extensions/msteams/src/file-consent.ts extensions/msteams/src/file-consent.test.ts extensions/msteams/src/request-timeout.test.ts` passed.
- `git diff --check` passed.
- Transfer-aware proof: `resolveMSTeamsSharePointUploadTimeoutMs(100 * 1024 * 1024)` now resolves to 700000ms: 300000ms base plus 400000ms transfer budget at 256KiB/s.
- Controlled upload-path proof: a 512KiB file-consent upload completed at 301000ms, after the old fixed 300000ms cutoff but before the size-derived deadline; the fetch signal remained un-aborted and the upload resolved.
- Stall proof retained: a controlled stalled consent upload aborts through `AbortSignal` and throws `MS Teams file consent upload timed out after 25ms`.
- Not run: live Microsoft Teams tenant / real SharePoint upload.

target.title: fix(minimax): resolve search env secret refs
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

`extensions/minimax/src/minimax-web-search-provider.runtime.ts` read MiniMax web-search credentials with `readConfiguredSecretString(...) ?? MINIMAX_*` env fallback. That path accepts direct strings, but an env SecretRef in `tools.web.search.apiKey` stays unresolved instead of reading the referenced environment variable.

## Why This Change Was Made

MiniMax web search already has several documented Token Plan/OAuth env fallbacks. A configured SecretRef should be resolved before those ambient fallbacks, and an unavailable SecretRef should fail closed instead of silently selecting `MINIMAX_CODE_PLAN_KEY`, `MINIMAX_CODING_API_KEY`, `MINIMAX_OAUTH_TOKEN`, or `MINIMAX_API_KEY`.

## User Impact

Users can keep MiniMax web-search keys in env-backed SecretRefs without storing raw credentials in config. If the referenced env var is absent, the tool reports the normal missing-key state rather than sending requests with an unrelated ambient MiniMax token.

## Evidence

- `OPENCLAW_HEAVY_CHECK_LOCK_SCOPE=worktree node scripts/run-vitest.mjs extensions/minimax/src/minimax-web-search-provider.test.ts -- --reporter=verbose` passed, 1 file / 21 tests.

## Proof

target.title: feat(ui): chat background-tasks rail detects running work eagerly and shows live tool activity
target.body:
Closes #104775

## What Problem This Solves

Resolves a problem where the chat pane's background-tasks rail could not detect running work until it was opened by hand: the task snapshot only loaded after the rail was first expanded, so the activity toggle never showed its running-count badge and running subagents/cron/CLI tasks stayed invisible in a fresh Control UI session.

Task rows were also opaque while work was running — just a status word, runtime family, and a relative start time ("Running · Subagent · 5m ago"), with no sense of how long the task has been running, how much it has done, or what it is doing right now.

## Why This Change Was Made

Detection is now owned by the task registry, which already observes every run's agent-event stream: tool starts increment a per-task `toolUseCount` and record `lastToolName` on the `TaskRecord`, persisted with the task row (additive `task_runs` columns + `ensureColumn` upgrade) and exposed as additive optional `TaskSummary` protocol fields, so `tasks.list`, `tasks.get`, `tasks.cancel`, and live `task` broadcasts all carry them. The Control UI loads the task snapshot eagerly (even while the rail is collapsed), folds `task` events that arrive before the snapshot into a load, and renders the richer rows; a small self-cleaning `openclaw-elapsed-time` element ticks the live timer. Token usage is intentionally out of scope — usage is not on the agent-event bus today.

## User Impact

- The activity toggle's running-count badge now appears as soon as background work exists, without opening the rail first — background tasks are detectable at a glance.
- Running rows show a live elapsed timer, tool-use count, and the tool currently in use; finished rows add the run duration.
- Works across subagent, cron, ACP, and CLI task runtimes; tool activity survives gateway restarts with the persisted task ledger.

## Evidence

Rail open with a running subagent (live elapsed, "12 tool uses", current tool `read`, progress line) and the collapsed-badge detection covered by e2e:

![rail open](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/steipete/openclaw-pr-assets/main/background-tasks-rail-activity/rail-open.png)

Pushed completion moves the row into Finished with its duration:

![pushed completion](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/steipete/openclaw-pr-assets/main/background-tasks-rail-activity/pushed-completion.png)

- `pnpm test src/tasks/task-registry.test.ts src/tasks/task-registry.store.test.ts src/gateway/server-methods/tasks.test.ts ui/src/pages/chat/components/chat-background-tasks.test.ts` — green (registry tool counting, sqlite persistence roundtrip, gateway summary mapping, UI eager load/badge/event-before-snapshot/row rendering).
- `pnpm test ui/src/pages/chat/background-tasks.e2e.test.ts` — green; now asserts the collapsed toggle badge shows the active count *before* the rail is opened, plus the tool-activity text in rows (screenshots above are its artifacts).
- Codex autoreview + `pnpm check:changed` run pre-push (results in PR comments/CI).

target.title: fix(apps): reconcile slow Apple chat replies
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

iOS and macOS chat treated a 30-second RPC deadline as the Gateway run deadline, while shared Apple chat also retired pending runs after a local 120-second timer. Slow first replies or reconnect/history gaps could therefore show a false timeout, clear the run owner early, or hide a later canonical reply.

## Why This Change Was Made

Ordinary Apple chat sends now omit `chat.send.timeoutMs`, leaving run lifetime with Gateway policy while retaining bounded request/ACK deadlines.

Shared Apple chat uses one arm-scoped owner per pending run. It combines route-bound `agent.wait` observations with bounded canonical-history polling, preserves terminal failures and Gateway error text, caches terminal state through reconnects, and keeps a short post-terminal history grace window before accepting a valid no-output completion. The owner holds the view model weakly and cancels both child paths together.

The rewrite intentionally does not change Android, Gateway schema, protocol version, configuration, provider routing, authentication, or persistence.

## User Impact

Slow accepted Apple chat replies stay pending until Gateway terminal state and canonical history reconcile. Missed lifecycle failures remain visible, reconnects cannot silently lose a known terminal result, and legitimate no-output completions still unblock sending.

## Evidence

- Exact rewritten head: `ddace4e9d2e60346edaaf8aed2019bba9f90f140`.
- Fresh autoreview completed clean after every actionable finding was fixed.

target.title: fix(agents): keep tool_search_code stderr tail UTF-16 safe
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

`tool_search_code` reports child exit failures by appending the last 500 UTF-16 code units of `stderrTail` to the error message. When that 500-unit boundary falls inside an astral character (emoji or other non-BMP text), the emitted error string contains an isolated surrogate half.

## Why This Change Was Made

The repository already has `sliceUtf16Safe` in `@openclaw/normalization-core/utf16-slice`, and an ongoing UTF-16 safe-truncation campaign has fixed the same pattern in bootstrap context (#104423), block chunks (#104441), failover details (#104487), and several other call sites. This change applies the same helper to the code-mode stderr tail path so error messages stay well-formed.

## User Impact

Error messages for failed `tool_search_code` executions that include non-BMP characters in stderr no longer contain malformed UTF-16 surrogate halves.

## Evidence

- Added a regression test in `src/agents/tool-search.stream-errors.test.ts` that emits stderr containing an emoji positioned so the raw `.slice(-500)` would produce a lone surrogate, and asserts the rejection message is well-formed.
- Local verification on current upstream `main`:
  - `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/agents/tool-search.stream-errors.test.ts --run` -> 2 passed
  - `node scripts/run-oxlint.mjs --tsconfig config/tsconfig/oxlint.core.json src/agents/tool-search.ts src/agents/tool-search.stream-errors.test.ts` -> exit code 0
  - `npx oxfmt --check --threads=1 src/agents/tool-search.ts src/agents/tool-search.stream-errors.test.ts` -> all matched files use correct format

## Competition / linked PR analysis

A fresh search found no open PR changing the stderr tail truncation in `src/agents/tool-search.ts` or the target regression test.

## Merge risk

- **Why it matters / User impact:** malformed UTF-16 in error strings can render as replacement characters or break later text handling.
- **Risk labels considered:** error-messages.
- **Risk explanation:** the tail may now end one code unit earlier when the 500-unit boundary bisects a surrogate pair. The error message remains human-readable and the total length stays bounded.

Related: #104318

## Maintainer decision (2026-07-12)

Approved to land by the maintainer with both consequences accepted explicitly: (1) existing flat-key configs become invalid at startup until `openclaw doctor --fix` (doctor config fixes are not auto-applied on startup; the existing "Legacy config keys detected" machinery names the exact keys and the fix command); (2) the runtime tolerance is removed ahead of the deprecation record's `removeAfter 2026-07-26` — deliberate acceleration; the doctor `--fix` migration itself is retained past that date.

## What Problem This Solves

Six legacy flat streaming keys (streamMode, chunkMode, blockStreaming, draftChunk, blockStreamingCoalesce, nativeStreaming) were normalized at steady-state load time, keeping non-canonical shapes alive in the runtime path against the repo's doctor-first rule (runtime reads canonical config only; older shapes migrate in doctor).

Load-time normalization for these keys is removed so runtime consumes only the nested `streaming.*` shape; `openclaw doctor --fix` migrates flat→nested for every channel that supports them. Filled coverage gaps: discord had a migration but no rules (added 2); imessage/msteams had neither (added rules+migrations). Fixed two shared-migration bugs found en route: flat keys weren't removed when the nested key was already set, and a streamMode-conflict removal produced empty changes that doctor discarded (leaving config invalid after --fix). Five channels keep flat keys canonical for now (signal, irc, googlechat, whatsapp, mattermost + the SDK reply-runtime shape) — documented follow-up territory, not silently dropped.

target.title: fix(memory): harden embedding batch workflows
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Embedding batch providers had several separate failure and output paths with inconsistent bounds, diagnostics, and terminal-state handling. Google-compatible endpoints could expose unbounded or ambiguous response handling, OpenAI and Voyage could inspect success output before completed error output, and memory-core had no typed way to disable a provider whose batch API is unavailable.

This supersedes the narrower fixes in #103306 and #98692.

## Why This Change Was Made

- Add one shared raw-byte JSONL reader with a 4 MiB record cap, physical-record budget, split UTF-8 support, early cancellation, and first-expected-response-wins semantics.
- Reuse that reader across Google, OpenAI, and Voyage instead of retaining provider-local parsers.
- Standardize bounded, redacted batch diagnostics and structured `ProviderHttpError` handling.
- Check completed error files before success output for OpenAI and Voyage.
- Align Google upload, operation state, output aliases, and download routing with the Gemini Batch API while preserving the shipped `file_name` request field.
- Add a typed `EmbeddingBatchUnavailableError` so memory-core can disable batch mode immediately after a Google batch-create 404.
- Refresh the plugin SDK API baseline and exact public-surface budgets for the new shared contract.

## User Impact

- Large valid JSONL outputs continue to stream without whole-file buffering.
- Oversized, malformed, duplicate, unknown, or excessive provider records fail closed and cancel the response stream.
- Provider diagnostics stay bounded and redact credential-like material.
- Completed provider errors are surfaced instead of being masked by output lookup.
- Google batch state and output discovery work across official Operation fields and shipped response aliases.
- Providers without a usable batch endpoint fall back immediately instead of retrying the unavailable path.

## Evidence

### Exact-head validation

- `git diff --check`
- `node scripts/plugin-sdk-surface-report.mjs --check`: 10,562 public exports and 5,255 callable exports, exactly matching the pinned budgets.
- Fresh autoreview after each final code/type/control-flow/budget correction: clean; no accepted or actionable findings.
- Sanitized AWS Crabbox `run_c0ec373344aa`: remote-child `pnpm check:changed` on exact head `b62ea06741f3c1cf37002326fbb082f7e0ed1329`; format, four type lanes, core lint, and extension lint passed. Its only failure was the unrelated Docker-E2E import boundary in `scripts/e2e/sqlite-sessions-transcripts-flip-proof.ts`, reproduced unchanged on clean current main `ff6dc43b8b8563f8bcc054c1430c980ecca66ae1`.
- Sanitized AWS Crabbox `run_8225acae277c`: 81 shared reader/error/status, SDK surface/baseline, and Google/OpenAI/Voyage batch assertions passed on the same exact head.
- Sanitized AWS Crabbox `run_ea1b83281790`: memory-core's immediate typed-unavailable fallback assertion passed on the same exact head.
- Hosted exact-head CI `29172170389`: 78 relevant checks passed, zero failed or pending; QA Smoke, lint, production/test types, security, and real-behavior checks were green.

### Real behavior proof

- The production Google batch path runs through a real loopback HTTP server for upload → batch create → status poll → split-chunk JSONL download. It verifies the official upload envelope, the shipped `file_name`, one credential across all four requests, and the returned embedding.
- Streaming tests exercise split UTF-8, CRLF, EOF, oversize cancellation, physical blank-row budgets, malformed/non-object JSON, duplicate/unknown IDs, and early callback termination.

Authenticated positive-job execution was not run: contributor/fork source is intentionally isolated from maintainer credentials. The real network lifecycle is covered against loopback, and the public Gemini contract was checked against the official Batch API guide and REST reference.

- https://ai.google.dev/gemini-api/docs/batch-api
- https://ai.google.dev/api/batch-api
- https://ai.google.dev/gemini-api/docs/troubleshooting

## Release note context

Harden embedding batch output and error handling across Google, OpenAI, and Voyage; improve Google Batch API compatibility and immediate fallback when batch creation is unavailable. Thanks @ZOOWH and @ly85206559 for the original reports and fixes.

target.title: fix(safeguard): resolve compaction provider/model before registering runtime
target.body:
Fixes #57901.

## What Problem This Solves

Normal safeguard auto-compaction still registers the active session model even when `agents.defaults.compaction.model` selects a different summarization target. Main's new route-aware auth planner fixed explicit compaction, but normal safeguard registration still ignored the override.

A safeguard override also needs its model route and credential to remain one atomic tuple. Binding a target credential into the active attempt registry can corrupt same-provider sessions before compaction starts.

## Summary

This refresh is merged with main at `266d49cddb977c45d40f13d27045214db29bc756` and adapts the safeguard override to the current route-aware runtime planner.

- Resolve the configured safeguard target before synchronous extension registration.
- Reuse an existing prepared auth plan only when it exactly matches the target provider/model.
- Otherwise prepare the target through the atomic runtime flow:
  `prepareAgentRuntimeAuth` → `materializePreparedRuntimeModel` → `resolvePreparedRuntimeAuthAttempts` → `resolvePreparedRuntimeModelAuth`.
- Preserve the selected model route, auth requirement, request transport overrides, runtime policy, selected profile, and credential as one tuple.
- Resolve the target with an isolated `AuthStorage`/`ModelRegistry`; never mutate the active attempt's auth registry.
- Carry the prepared model, target registry, and resolved auth plan through the safeguard runtime registry.
- Prefer the prepared safeguard model and its paired registry in the hook.
- Reject prepared routes whose runtime policy does not support the OpenClaw runtime.
- Preserve locked native-harness sessions on their pinned model.
- Warn and fall back to the active model when the configured target cannot be resolved or authenticated.
- Keep explicit compaction on main's current prepared-route implementation while forwarding its resolved model, registry, and auth plan into safeguard runtime state.

## Safety Invariants

- A same-provider override using a different profile cannot replace the active session key.
- Cross-provider model, API, base URL, route requirement, transport overrides, runtime policy, selected profile, and key are resolved together.
- The safeguard hook looks up target credentials in the target registry, not the active attempt registry.
- `buildEmbeddedExtensionFactories` remains synchronous by receiving a precomputed target.

## Evidence

Validated on exact local tree `b38eded0065419c75b3b1f369b96d7359c0cb239`:

target.title: Propagate AbortSignal through bundle MCP tool/resource/prompt calls
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

When an agent run is cancelled, pending bundle MCP tool/resource/prompt requests keep running because the per-call `AbortSignal` is dropped after `AgentTool.execute`. This leaves MCP child work alive after the caller has aborted, wastes resources, and can produce late results that race with cleanup.

## Why This Change Was Made

PR #104110 fixed the same issue for bundle LSP JSON-RPC requests by forwarding the `AbortSignal` and emitting `$/cancelRequest`. Bundle MCP uses the same `AgentTool.execute` contract but ignores the signal all the way down to the MCP SDK client. This change plumbs the signal through the same layers so MCP requests can be cancelled.

## User Impact

- Cancelling an agent turn or session now stops pending bundle MCP tool calls, resource reads, and prompt fetches instead of letting them run to completion.
- Reduces wasted compute and prevents late MCP responses from being applied after cancellation.

## Evidence

- Added a regression test in `src/agents/agent-bundle-mcp-tools.materialize.test.ts` that verifies the `AbortSignal` is forwarded from each projected tool's `execute` into `runtime.callTool`, `listResources`, `readResource`, `listPrompts`, and `getPrompt`.
- Existing tests pass:

target.title: fix(agents): surface utility-model narration failures and show the utility model in models status
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Utility-model narration (#103463, #103769) fails silently when its credential is dead. Observed live on the Molty gateway: the primary model rides Codex OAuth, but the derived utility model (`openai/gpt-5.6-luna`) resolves the `openai:api-key` auth profile, which held a revoked key. Every narration call 401ed, the narrator disabled itself after 2 consecutive failures, and Discord kept showing the old raw tool lines — with zero operator-visible signal:

- narrator failures were `logVerbose`-only, and the log line did not name the agent, model, or auth profile;
- `openclaw models status` never mentioned the utility model, so nothing showed that narration depends on a different auth path than the primary.

Fixes #104764.

## Why This Change Was Made

A dead utility credential silently degrades the product experience (narrated progress drafts fall back to raw tool lines). The failure needs to be visible at default log levels and the utility model needs to be inspectable in `models status`, which owns runtime auth visibility (`--probe`/`--check`).

## User Impact

- When narration disables after consecutive failures, the gateway now logs one warn per turn: `narration disabled after 2 consecutive failures (openai/gpt-5.6-luna via openai:api-key): OpenAI API error (401): …` — naming exactly what to repair.
- `openclaw models status` shows a `Utility model` line (explicit config / provider default / disabled) and a `utilityModel: { ref, source }` field in `--json`.

## Evidence

- Live root-cause log (Molty gateway, 2026-07-11 22:25Z): `progress-narrator: completion failed: OpenAI API error (401): 401 Incorrect API key provided: sk-proj-…` repeated per turn while Discord rendered old-style tool lines; details in #104764.
- Testbox (blacksmith, lease `tbx_01kx9pjsm0ct72rze4k3ks3zzh`, [run](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/29171446325)): `pnpm format:check` green; `pnpm test src/auto-reply/reply/progress-narrator.test.ts src/commands/models/list.status.test.ts` → 15 + 34 tests pass, including the new warn assertion and the new `utilityModel` JSON cases (explicit config and disabled).

Follow-up tracked separately in #104764: `models status --probe` routes `api_key`-profile probes through the codex app-server harness, which cannot validate an API key (needs the Codex-contract review gate).

target.title: fix(telegram): preserve Codex login profile identity
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes #104704.

Telegram `/login codex` could complete a Codex/OpenAI device-code login for a different OpenAI account while persisting the refreshed OAuth credential under the previously selected auth profile id. That left status/listing surfaces looking pinned to the old account and let cooldown/usage state stay attached to the stale profile key.

This is a narrow identity-boundary fix. The broader multi-profile cooldown/fallback behavior is still tracked separately in #99684, #97764, #83496, #70903, and related auth-wedge issues.

## Why This Change Was Made

The Telegram native `/login codex` path was resolving the target session's current `authProfileOverride` and passing it into the provider login flow as `profileId`. That forced `src/commands/models/auth.ts` to persist the new OAuth result under the old profile id, overriding the canonical id derived from the newly authenticated account.

This PR changes that flow so Telegram `/login codex`:

- lets the provider login return the canonical profile id for the authenticated account,
- moves the target Telegram session to that returned profile id after login succeeds,
- treats that session metadata update as best-effort so a session-store write failure does not incorrectly report that OAuth login failed,
- narrows the Codex device-login runtime return type to `ModelsAuthLoginFlowResult` so callers can safely inspect returned profiles.

## User Impact

After pairing a different OpenAI account via `/login codex`, the current Telegram session should follow the newly authenticated Codex/OpenAI profile instead of staying pinned to the old profile id/label.

This should also prevent usage/cooldown state from being accidentally associated with the stale profile id during account switches.

## Evidence

Focused local checks:

```bash
node scripts/run-vitest.mjs extensions/telegram/src/bot-native-commands.session-meta.test.ts
node scripts/run-vitest.mjs extensions/telegram/src/bot-native-commands.login.test.ts
git diff --check
```

target.title: feat(memory): add multi-slot memory role architecture
target.body:
## Summary

This PR fixes a memory-plugin architecture flaw: OpenClaw currently has one exclusive `plugins.slots.memory` owner even though the product, docs, bundled plugins, and runtime behavior already treat “memory” as several different responsibilities.

Today, factual recall, auto-capture, compaction, dreaming/consolidation, and user/session modeling are all forced through the same global selector. That makes documented memory stacks impossible or brittle: selecting one memory provider can unintentionally displace another provider that owns a different responsibility.

This PR corrects that mismatch by introducing purpose-specific memory role slots:

- `memory.recall`
- `memory.capture`
- `memory.compaction`
- `memory.dreaming`
- `memory.userModel`

The new role slots are the mechanism. The fix is that OpenClaw can now represent the memory architecture it already documents and partially implements.

## What Problem This Solves

This is a flaw fix, not just a feature request.

OpenClaw’s memory ecosystem is already multi-role:

- `memory-core` / QMD provide local factual recall/search over project memory, session transcripts, and Markdown/QMD corpora.
- Honcho provides cross-session user, agent, and session modeling.
- LanceDB provides embedding-backed long-term recall and auto-capture.
- Active Memory orchestrates recall before generation by using whichever provider owns recall.
- Memory Wiki compiles durable memory into a companion knowledge vault rather than replacing active memory.
- Dreaming/consolidation is a separate runtime responsibility from ordinary recall.

The current `plugins.slots.memory` contract cannot express that architecture. It treats every `kind: "memory"` provider as competing for one owner slot, even when the providers are designed to do different jobs. That leads to three concrete problems:

1. **Documented combinations are not representable.** Configs such as builtin/QMD recall + Honcho user modeling, LanceDB capture + local recall, or Active Memory over a selected recall provider cannot be modeled cleanly through one memory owner.
2. **Runtime behavior depends on exceptions and side paths.** Plugins that should compose have to rely on context-engine ownership, sidecar behavior, fallback logic, or plugin-specific handling instead of a shared contract.
3. **Diagnostics and lifecycle handling become misleading.** Startup, validation, status, doctor repair, skill publishing, uninstall cleanup, runtime memory resolution, and SDK-facing aliases need to know which provider owns which memory responsibility.

So while this PR adds new public config keys, the intent is corrective: make the config/runtime contract match the memory system OpenClaw already exposes.

## User Impact / Intended Outcome

After this PR, OpenClaw can express memory stacks that were previously documented or implied but not cleanly configurable:

- `memory-core` or QMD can own factual recall while Honcho owns user/session modeling.
- LanceDB can own recall and/or capture without forcing unrelated memory roles through the same selector.
- Active Memory can use the configured `memory.recall` provider instead of depending on hard-coded assumptions.
- Dreaming/consolidation can be selected separately from ordinary recall where supported.
- Memory Wiki can remain a companion compiled-knowledge layer beside active memory providers.
- Existing configs using `plugins.slots.memory` continue to work as recall selection.
- `openclaw doctor --fix` can migrate/canonicalize non-conflicting legacy memory-slot config while preserving the legacy key for plugin compatibility.

## Linked Context

Closes #60572.

Directly related memory-composition requests and prior proposals:

- #38874: supplementary/additive memory plugins alongside the primary memory slot.
- #2306: earlier closed PR proposing stackable memory plugins.
- #2080: earlier request for multiple simultaneous memory plugins and emerging memory architectures.
- #77714: pluggable persistent memory backend demand.

Dreaming and memory-role separation context:

- #85473: future protocol work for making dreaming implementable by non-`memory-core` memory plugins. This PR adds the `memory.dreaming` slot contract but does not implement that full protocol.
- #63067 and #65411: prior work around keeping dreaming behavior available when another plugin owns the legacy memory slot.
- #62275: previous selected-slot dreaming config behavior.

Runtime/diagnostic slot handling context:

- #76567 and #76495: configured memory-slot runtime checks should load/consult the selected memory plugin.
- #78540: doctor/status memory diagnostics could misreport configured memory providers.
- #76550: stale `plugins.slots.*` references could leave config unrecoverable until doctor cleanup was broadened.

Context-engine compatibility context:

- #77063, #77185, #76576, and #81843: context-engine registration and LosslessClaw-adjacent failures shaped the compatibility review for preserving the existing global `plugins.slots.contextEngine` behavior while rejecting unsupported per-agent `contextEngine` config.

Future API/RFC context:

- #70823: future machine-readable slot ownership/provenance. This PR intentionally keeps scalar plugin IDs and solves the memory role composition layer first.

Memory-plugin interop research: the [supporting research document](https://github.com/kklouzal/rfcs/blob/rfc/multi-slot-memory-role-architecture/rfcs/0009/memory-plugin-interop-research.md) validates this PR as necessary architecture work, not optional extensibility: OpenClaw's own documentation already describes memory as a composable ecosystem where builtin/QMD recall, Honcho user/session modeling, LanceDB recall/capture, Active Memory orchestration, dreaming/consolidation, and Memory Wiki compilation can coexist, but current `origin/main` collapses every `kind: "memory"` provider into one exclusive `plugins.slots.memory` owner, making those documented combinations impossible or dependent on brittle exceptions. PR #88504 closes that product/docs/runtime gap by replacing the single memory owner with explicit role slots — `memory.recall`, `memory.capture`, `memory.compaction`, `memory.dreaming`, and `memory.userModel` — while preserving legacy `memory` as a recall shorthand, so the documented memory-plugin interop story becomes actually representable in config and runtime behavior.

## What Changes

- Adds canonical memory role slots: `memory.recall`, `memory.capture`, `memory.compaction`, `memory.dreaming`, and `memory.userModel`.
- Keeps legacy `plugins.slots.memory` as a backward-compatible shorthand for `memory.recall` during an extended migration window.
- Adds per-agent memory role-slot overrides under `agents.list[*].plugins.slots`, limited to memory roles plus legacy `memory`.
- Wires role-slot selection through config schema/types/help/docs, plugin activation, gateway startup preloading, runtime memory resolution, skill publishing, validation, doctor repair/preview, uninstall cleanup, status diagnostics, and SDK-facing aliases.
- Preserves the existing global `plugins.slots.contextEngine` path for LosslessClaw and other context-engine plugins.
- Explicitly rejects unsupported per-agent `agents.list[*].plugins.slots.contextEngine` overrides because agent-scoped context-engine semantics are outside this PR.

## Implementation Notes

- Adds `src/plugins/slot-resolution.ts` as the shared role-slot helper layer for canonical memory role keys, defaults, normalization, effective per-agent resolution, and configured selection collection.
- Updates config schema/types/help/labels/docs for global and per-agent memory role slots.
- Keeps `PluginSlotsConfig.contextEngine` for global plugin slots, and adds an agent-slot type/schema that omits `contextEngine`.
- Updates doctor legacy memory-slot handling so `doctor --fix` canonicalizes to `memory.recall` while retaining legacy `memory` during the compatibility window.
- Updates plugin loader/activation/startup resolution so explicit role-slot selections activate memory plugins without confusing default `memory-core` fallback with a user-selected plugin under restrictive allowlists.
- Extends validation to report missing role-slot plugin refs and validate schemas for plugins selected only by non-recall or per-agent memory roles.
- Extends skill publishing, status scanning, uninstall cleanup, memory runtime, dreaming, compaction provider, and SDK alias behavior to use the role-aware model.
- Keeps memory runtime registrations addressable by plugin id, so runtime recall dispatch follows the resolved global or per-agent `memory.recall` owner.
- Passes the session agent id into Pi embedded extension factory construction so safeguard compaction provider selection honors per-agent `memory.compaction` overrides in both normal session runs and manual/queued compaction paths.
- Updates bundled memory plugin manifests/docs to describe role support and the recall shorthand migration.

target.title: fix(tts): defer text settlement for final-mode TTS to eliminate churn (#83511)
target.body:
## Summary

When `messages.tts.mode = "final"`, the Telegram bot exhibited text "churn" — users would briefly see a text message appear, then it would be deleted and replaced by a voice note with the same text as caption. This happened on **both** the ACP dispatch path and the non-ACP dispatch path (`dispatch-from-config.ts`).

This PR eliminates the churn on **both paths** by introducing a `captionedFinalText` channel capability, suppressing live block delivery and partial streaming when captioned final TTS will be used, and correctly handling tagged auto-TTS mode with a split eligibility boolean.

## Root cause

```
Before (main):
  1. Block text / partial streaming delivers text to user immediately
  2. TTS synthesis runs (2-5 seconds)
  3. Voice note + caption delivered as separate message
  Result: user sees text first, then voice note = churn (#83511)

After (this PR):
  1. willUseCaptionedFinalTts = true (channel supports captioned voice + final TTS mode)
  2. Partial streaming suppressed, block text delivery suppressed
  3. TTS synthesis runs, text accumulated silently
  4. Voice note + caption delivered as single message (or text fallback if TTS fails)
  Result: user sees only the voice note with caption = no churn
```

### Tagged auto-TTS mode

When `messages.tts.auto: "tagged"`, TTS only fires for replies containing `[[tts:...]]` directives. Three additional issues were discovered and fixed:

1. **Split boolean**: `willUseCaptionedFinalTts` was doing two jobs — gating live text suppression AND caption eligibility. Split into `willUseCaptionedFinalTts` (live text suppression, excludes tagged) and `canCaptionFinalTts` (caption eligibility, includes tagged).

2. **Block TTS gate**: The accumulated block TTS fallback was gated on `replies.length === 0`, but Anthropic streaming returns both block callbacks and a final reply payload. Changed to gate on `deliveredFinalTtsMedia` and `queuedFinal` instead.

3. **Partial streaming leak**: `onPartialReply` was active for tagged mode, sending raw `[[tts:text]]...[[/tts:text]]` directive text to Telegram during streaming, creating a duplicate text message before the voice+caption arrived. Fixed by gating `onPartialReply` with `canCaptionFinalTts` (covers both always and tagged modes) instead of `willUseCaptionedFinalTts`.

### Media block preservation

When captioned final TTS is active, block suppression is narrowed to **text-only** payloads. Blocks containing media (`mediaUrl`, `mediaUrls`), `presentation`, `interactive`, or `channelData` are delivered immediately with their text stripped (to avoid duplicating the caption). This applies to both ACP and non-ACP dispatch paths.

## Changes

| File | Change |
|------|--------|
| `src/auto-reply/reply/dispatch-from-config.ts` | `willUseCaptionedFinalTts` + `canCaptionFinalTts`: suppress partial streaming and block text for both always and tagged modes; narrow block suppression to text-only payloads (media blocks delivered with text stripped); `sendFinalPayload` returns `deliveredMedia`; block TTS gate changed from `replies.length === 0` to `!deliveredFinalTtsMedia && !queuedFinal` |
| `src/auto-reply/reply/dispatch-from-config.test.ts` | Regression tests: tagged directive-only voice+caption, tagged+always both-block-and-final delivery, partial suppression for tagged TTS on caption-capable channels, plain tagged block delivery, media block delivery with text stripped, text-only block suppression |
| `src/auto-reply/reply/dispatch-acp.ts` | `willUseCaptionedFinalTts` gate: suppress ACP block delivery and defer text settlement; `canCaptionFinalTts` for tagged mode; `deliveredFinalTtsMedia` tracking |
| `src/auto-reply/reply/dispatch-acp-delivery.ts` | `deliveredFinalTtsMedia` state tracking + `hasDeliveredFinalTtsMedia()` accessor; narrow `suppressBlockUserDelivery` to text-only blocks (media blocks delivered with text stripped) |
| `src/auto-reply/reply/dispatch-acp-delivery.test.ts` | Regression tests: media block delivery with text stripped under `suppressBlockUserDelivery`, text-only block suppression |
| `src/auto-reply/reply/dispatch-acp.test.ts` | Regression tests: deferred settlement, block suppression, tagged streaming, tagged directive TTS, ACP live text deferral |
| `src/auto-reply/reply/acp-projector.ts` | `deferLiveTextUntilFinalFlush` option to suppress live text flushing for tagged TTS |
| `src/tts/directives.ts` | `resolveDirectiveOnlyTtsCaptionText` parser helper to extract clean caption from directive-only responses |
| `extensions/telegram/src/shared.ts` | `captionedFinalText: true` capability declaration |
| `extensions/telegram/src/shared.test.ts` | Test for capability declaration |
| `src/channels/plugins/types.core.ts` | JSDoc for `captionedFinalText` capability contract |
| `src/channels/plugins/tts-capabilities.test.ts` | Capability seam test |
| `docs/tools/tts.md` | Document `captionedFinalText` capability: opt-in criteria via `capabilities.tts.voice`, tagged mode behavior, text-only fallback, plugin API snippet |
| `docs/plugins/sdk-channel-plugins.md` | Document `captionedFinalText` capability in channel plugin SDK guide: opt-in declaration, media block preservation, fallback behavior, tagged mode |
| `docs/.generated/plugin-sdk-api-baseline.sha256` | Updated SDK API baseline hash |

## Tests

```
$ npx vitest run src/auto-reply/reply/dispatch-from-config.test.ts
 ✓ 272 passed (272)

$ npx vitest run src/auto-reply/reply/dispatch-acp-delivery.test.ts
 ✓ 38 passed (38)

$ npx vitest run src/auto-reply/reply/dispatch-acp.test.ts
 ✓ 67 passed (67)

$ npx vitest run src/auto-reply/reply/dispatch-from-config.reply-dispatch.test.ts src/auto-reply/reply/dispatch-from-config.final-outcome-counts.test.ts src/auto-reply/reply/dispatch-from-config.acp-abort.test.ts
 ✓ 26 passed (26)   # settle-lifecycle paths, no hang

$ npx vitest run extensions/telegram/src/shared.test.ts
 ✓ 11 passed (11)

$ npx vitest run src/channels/plugins/tts-capabilities.test.ts
 ✓ 1 passed (1)
```

## Real behavior proof

- **Behavior or issue addressed**: Telegram TTS final-mode text-before-voice churn on both ACP and non-ACP dispatch paths, plus tagged mode partial preview leaking raw `[[tts:text]]` directives, plus media block suppression during captioned final TTS.

- **Real environment tested**: Local patched OpenClaw checkout at commit `05b4483a8f`, macOS arm64, Node.js v24.10.0. Live Telegram bot (`@thomas_fu_bot`) with Microsoft TTS (`zh-CN-XiaoxiaoNeural`), `messages.tts.mode: "final"`.

- **Failing proof before fix (live Telegram)**:

  ![Before fix — separate text message + voice message (churn)](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Jerry-Xin/openclaw/proof-images-83988/.proof-images/83988-before-fix.png)

  User sent "hello" to the Telegram bot. The bot responded with **two separate messages**: a text message AND a voice note — instead of a single voice note with caption.

- **Exact steps or command run after this patch**:
  1. Built and installed from current head: `npm run build && npm pack && npm install -g openclaw-2026.6.2.tgz`
  2. Registered and restarted Gateway: `openclaw gateway install && openclaw gateway restart`
  3. Tested with `messages.tts.auto: "always"` and `messages.tts.auto: "tagged"` — sent plain messages and directive-bearing messages to `@thomas_fu_bot` on Telegram

- **Evidence after fix**: Always mode (`messages.tts.auto: "always"`) at commit `05b4483a8f`:

  ![Always mode — voice with caption, single message](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Jerry-Xin/openclaw/proof-images-83988/.proof-images/83988-always-mode.png)

  Always-mode replies produce a single voice note with caption text. No text churn, no separate text bubble.

- **Evidence — Media block preservation with captioned final TTS at commit `05b4483a8f`**:

  ![Media block preserved — image delivered + voice note with caption](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Jerry-Xin/openclaw/proof-images-83988/.proof-images/83988-media-block.png)

  When the bot generates an image during a TTS-enabled conversation (`auto: "always"`), the image is delivered immediately while text is deferred to the voice note caption. No media blocks are suppressed, and caption text does not duplicate as a separate text message.

- **Observed result after fix**: Always TTS auto mode delivers voice notes as single messages with caption text on Telegram. Media blocks (images, files) are preserved and delivered immediately with text stripped. No text flash, no duplicate messages, no media loss.

- **What was not tested**: Other TTS providers (only Microsoft TTS tested live). Group chat TTS (tested in DM only). Other channels with `captionedFinalText` capability (only Telegram tested). Tagged mode live proof pending — covered by unit tests (partial suppression + directive-only caption regression tests added).

## Settle-lifecycle reconciliation (rebased onto current main)

Current `main` made the delivered-transcript mirror fire-and-forget so reply completion no longer blocks on `dispatcher.waitForIdle()`. An earlier revision of this PR gated the captioned-final text fallback on an inline `await dispatcher.waitForIdle()` inside the reply operation, which would reintroduce exactly that completion-vs-idle block.

The fallback rides the same dispatcher settle lifecycle instead of an inline wait, and it is attributed **per captioned voice payload** rather than by aggregate dispatcher counters:

- Each captioned final (and its synthesized-voice sibling) is tagged with a unique capture token stored in the payload metadata, which survives the dispatcher's internal re-normalization.
- Before enqueue, a per-payload cancelled hook and a per-payload delivery-failed hook are registered, both keyed to that capture token. The delivery-failed hook (`appendReplyDispatcherBeforeDeliverFailed`) is a core-internal observer symmetric to the existing per-payload cancelled hook — it is not part of the plugin-facing dispatcher surface.
- A post-settlement task registered via `registerReplyDispatcherSettledTask` (the same seam the transcript mirror uses) runs after `waitForIdle()` inside `settleReplyDispatcher`, out of the reply hot path. It re-sends the accumulated block text as a text-only final **if and only if this specific captioned voice's own send was cancelled or failed** — never based on the aggregate final-outcome delta.

This matters because a single reply can enqueue multiple finals (a captioned voice plus sibling reasoning/commentary/status finals). The previous aggregate-count comparison mis-attributed a sibling final's failure or cancellation to the captioned voice, re-sending text the voice note had already delivered as its caption — reintroducing the exact churn this PR removes. Per-payload attribution fixes that: recovery follows the captioned voice's own outcome, mirroring the per-send attribution the ACP path already uses. A mixed-outcome regression asserts that a captioned voice which succeeds while a sibling final fails does **not** re-send the caption text. This preserves the churn fix and the async-failure text fallback while keeping reply completion off `waitForIdle`, so the fire-and-forget contract from the current transcript-mirror behavior is not regressed.

### Cancelled final delivery (not just failed)

A `beforeDeliver` / `reply_payload_sending` hook returning `null` **cancels** a send after `enqueue()` has already reported acceptance. That outcome is tracked as *cancelled*, not *failed* (`getCancelledCounts()` vs `getFailedCounts()` on the dispatcher). The ACP direct-visible-text settlement previously folded only failed counts into its undelivered accounting, so a cancelled captioned voice final left `finalMediaDelivered` set and skipped the deferred text fallback — silently dropping the reply text (the block text was already suppressed for the captioned path).

The settlement now folds cancelled block/final counts alongside failed counts (`settleDirectVisibleText` in `dispatch-acp-delivery.ts`, via a new `readDispatcherCancelledCounts` reader mirroring the failed reader). A cancelled captioned voice final therefore clears `finalMediaDelivered` and the deferred text fallback delivers the accumulated text. The non-ACP path now applies the same per-payload cancelled/failed attribution described above (a cancelled captioned voice recovers its text; a sibling's cancellation does not). A regression test drives an asynchronously cancelled captioned voice on Telegram and asserts the plain-text fallback fires.

Closes #83511

target.title: fix(channels): fix five channel lifecycle/shutdown bugs
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves
Five small channel reliability bugs where lifecycle/shutdown paths can leak timers, unhandled rejections, or ignore abort signals.

1. **iMessage RPC client** `stop()` left a 500ms SIGTERM fallback timer running when the child process had already exited, keeping the event loop alive unnecessarily.
2. **Telegram webhook** shutdown could produce an unhandled promise rejection if `bot.stop()` or transport close threw inside the abort listener.
3. **Telegram ingress worker** `stop()` was not idempotent and could leak a second 15s terminate timer; `worker.terminate()` rejections were unhandled.
4. **Telegram probe** transport cache eviction closed the oldest transport with `void transport.close()`, so a rejecting `close()` became an unhandled rejection.
5. **ClickClack gateway** reconnect backoff used a raw `setTimeout` that ignored `abortSignal`, so stopping the gateway could wait the full reconnect delay. It also leaked an abort listener on every normal reconnect.

## Why This Change Was Made
- iMessage: store the fallback timer, `unref` it, and clear it once the child-close race settles.
- Telegram webhook: catch shutdown errors inside the abort paths, route them to `runtime.error`, and continue owned transport/status cleanup even if `bot.stop()` rejects.
- Telegram ingress worker: guard `stop()` with a `stopped` flag and catch `worker.terminate()` rejections.
- Telegram probe: wrap the close result with `Promise.resolve(...).catch(...)` so both sync and async rejections are swallowed safely.
- ClickClack gateway: reconnect backoff uses the shared `sleepWithAbort` from `openclaw/plugin-sdk/runtime-env`, treating abort rejection as normal gateway termination instead of a local timer/listener.
- Telegram probe test: use `vi.stubEnv` for `NODE_ENV`/`VITEST` so Vitest teardown restores them, instead of direct `process.env` assignment that leaked production-mode values to worker siblings.

This update also fixes the `check-test-types` failures reported by ClawSweeper (iMessage child mock typing and ClickClack config narrowing) and strengthens the iMessage test to assert the timer is cleared immediately on settlement, not only after it would have fired.

## User Impact
Cleaner shutdown for channel gateways and fewer uncaught/unhandled rejection crashes during abort, restart, or transport eviction.

## Real behavior proof

**Environment:** Linux, Node v22.22.0, pnpm 11.2.2.

The proof now includes a standalone real-gateway run for the ClickClack reconnect backoff fix (local HTTP + WebSocket servers driving the real `startClickClackGatewayAccount` production function), plus the regression-test negative controls used earlier.

### ClickClack gateway: real reconnect run with local servers

This script starts real local HTTP and WebSocket servers, configures `startClickClackGatewayAccount` to point at them, waits for the websocket cycle to start, forces a reconnect, then aborts. With the fix the gateway run resolves in ~50 ms instead of waiting the configured 60 s reconnect delay.

```bash
node --import tsx proof-clickclack-reconnect.mts
```

```typescript
import { createServer } from "node:http";
import { AddressInfo } from "node:net";
import { WebSocket, WebSocketServer } from "ws";
import type { ChannelGatewayContext } from "openclaw/plugin-sdk/channel-contract";
import { startClickClackGatewayAccount } from "./extensions/clickclack/src/gateway.js";
import type { ResolvedClickClackAccount } from "./extensions/clickclack/src/types.js";

function assert(description: string, condition: boolean) {
  if (condition) console.log(`  ok: ${description}`);
  else { console.log(`  FAIL: ${description}`); process.exitCode = 1; }
}

async function startClickClackMockServers() {
  const connections: WebSocket[] = [];
  const httpServer = createServer((req, res) => {
    const url = new URL(req.url ?? "/", `http://localhost`);
    res.setHeader("Content-Type", "application/json");
    if (url.pathname === "/api/me") {
      res.end(JSON.stringify({ user: { id: "bot-1", display_name: "Bot", handle: "bot", avatar_url: "", created_at: "2026-01-01T00:00:00.000Z" } }));
    } else if (url.pathname === "/api/realtime/events") {
      res.end(JSON.stringify({ events: [] }));
    } else {
      res.statusCode = 404;
      res.end(JSON.stringify({ error: "not found" }));
    }
  });
  const wss = new WebSocketServer({ server: httpServer });
  wss.on("connection", (ws) => { connections.push(ws); });
  await new Promise<void>((resolve) => httpServer.listen(0, "127.0.0.1", resolve));
  const addr = httpServer.address() as AddressInfo;
  return { httpUrl: `http://127.0.0.1:${addr.port}`, httpServer, wss, connections };
}

async function main() {
  const { httpUrl, httpServer, wss, connections } = await startClickClackMockServers();
  const abort = new AbortController();
  const ctx: ChannelGatewayContext<ResolvedClickClackAccount> = {
    cfg: { channels: { clickclack: { baseUrl: httpUrl, token: "test-token", workspace: "wsp_test", reconnectMs: 60_000 } } } as any,
    accountId: "default",
    account: {} as ResolvedClickClackAccount,
    runtime: {} as any,
    abortSignal: abort.signal,
    log: { warn: () => {}, info: () => {}, error: () => {}, debug: () => {} },
    getStatus: () => ({ accountId: "default" }) as any,
    setStatus: () => {},
  };

  const start = Date.now();
  const runPromise = startClickClackGatewayAccount(ctx);

  await new Promise<void>((resolve) => {
    const check = setInterval(() => { if (connections.length > 0) { clearInterval(check); resolve(); } }, 10);
  });

  for (const ws of connections) ws.close();
  abort.abort();
  await runPromise;
  const elapsed = Date.now() - start;

  assert(`gateway run resolved in under 5s (actual ${elapsed}ms)`, elapsed < 5_000);

  httpServer.close();
  wss.close();
  console.log("\nPROOF ASSERTIONS: all passed");
}

main().catch((err) => { console.error(err); process.exit(1); });
```

```text
=== ClickClack reconnect backoff real behavior proof ===
Node: v22.22.0

[case 1] startClickClackGatewayAccount aborts promptly during reconnect backoff
  ok: gateway run resolved in under 5s (actual 50ms)
  ok: reconnectMs was 60s, so a raw setTimeout would have hung

[case 2] raw setTimeout reconnect wait ignores abort (negative control)
  ok: raw setTimeout wait did NOT resolve early (actual 5002ms >= 4500ms)

=== Summary ===
PROOF ASSERTIONS: all passed
```

The second case demonstrates the old raw-`setTimeout` behavior: aborting has no effect, so the wait continues for the full delay. The first case shows the fixed production gateway reacting to abort immediately while a real reconnect delay is pending.

target.title: fix(imessage): apply authoritative projection in anchorless recovery
target.body:
Fixes openclaw/openclaw#104136

## What Problem This Solves

`repairIMessageConversationAnchor()` recovered conversation anchors from exact-GUID `messages.history` rows but only overlaid `chat_id` / `chat_guid` / `chat_identifier`. It preserved stale notification `sender`, `destination_caller_id`, and `is_from_me`, which could:

1. Route a direct reply at the local iMessage identity instead of the remote peer.
2. Dispatch an outgoing row as inbound when history says `is_from_me: true` but the broken notification said `false`.

## Changes

- Build a complete **authoritative recovery projection** from exact-GUID history rows (sender, direction, conversation fields).
- **Keep `destination_caller_id` optional** per imsg payload contract.
- **Fail-closed** on incomplete/conflicting projections; **drop recovered `is_from_me: true` rows**.

## Evidence

**Current head:** `577af515`

| Layer | Case | Result |
|-------|------|--------|
| L1 | issue synthetic repro: stale sender → authoritative remote sender | pass |
| L1 | history omits `destination_caller_id` | pass |
| L1 | history `is_from_me: true` with notification `false` | dropped |
| L1 | conflicting exact-GUID rows | dropped |
| L2 | repair → inbound decision → `buildIMessageInboundContext` | `To=imessage:+15550000002` |
| L3 | `monitorIMessageProvider` + issue payloads: remote reply routing | `ctx.To=imessage:+15550000002` |

target.title: fix(workboard): resolve parent dependency status via targeted lookups, not a full-corpus scan
target.body:
### Problem

`WorkboardStore.dependencyTargetStatus()` (`extensions/workboard/src/store.ts`)
checks whether a card's parent(s) are `done` before promoting it out of a
dependency-held status. To do that, it called the fully **unscoped**
`this.list()` — every card, on every board, fully materialized via
`entries()` + `readCard()` — and built a `Map` from it, just to look up 1-2
parent ids.

`dispatch()` calls `promoteDependencyReady()` (which calls
`dependencyTargetStatus()`) once per card in its board-scoped dispatch pass.
So every parented card being checked in a single dispatch pass re-paid for a
full-corpus re-scan: **O(parented_cards_in_pass × total_corpus_size ×
queries_per_card)**. `readCard()` alone issues 4 separate synchronous SQL
statements per row (metadata, events, child rows, labels), so on a
multi-thousand-row corpus this is thousands of synchronous SQL round-trips
per dispatch pass, once per parented card.

### How this was found

Root-caused via a live CDP CPU profile of a real, reproducible
`openclaw workboard dispatch --board <board>` call that was taking 160s+
wall-clock on a corpus of ~5770 cards, despite the dispatch handler's own
instrumented pass timers reporting well under 1 second. Attached Node's
inspector (`--inspect`) to the already-running gateway process, used
`Profiler.start`/`Profiler.stop` over the CDP protocol scoped exactly around
a real reproduction of the stall (161.8s elapsed, matching the known
symptom), and analyzed the resulting `.cpuprofile`.

**93.3% of the profiled wall-clock time** (142s self-time in a native `all()`
binding + 8.7s in `prepare()`, out of 162s total) was attributed to one call
chain:

```
dispatch()
  -> promoteDependencyReady()
    -> dependencyTargetStatus()
      -> list()
        -> entries()
          -> readCard()  (4 sync SQL statements per row)
```

This ruled out the leading working theory for this class of symptom (generic
Node event-loop starvation from a concurrent embedded/CLI agent session
monopolizing the process, as tracked in #84903 / #101895) — for this
specific, reproducible stall, the entire cost is inside the dispatch call's
own synchronous execution, not contention with unrelated work. The call
stack's `runMicrotasks → processTicksAndRejections → (root)` frames above the
hot path are simply how V8's CPU profiler represents async/await
continuations between awaited promises; they are not evidence of a different
concurrent job running.

### Fix

Replace the unscoped `list()` + `Map` lookup with targeted `get(parentId)`
calls — `get()` is already a single indexed-row lookup
(`this.store.lookup(id)`) used everywhere else in this file:

```ts
// before
const cards = new Map((await this.list()).map((entry) => [entry.id, entry]));
const parentsDone = parents.every((parentId) => cards.get(parentId)?.status === "done");

// after
const parentCards = await Promise.all(parents.map((parentId) => this.get(parentId)));
const parentsDone = parentCards.every((parent) => parent?.status === "done");
```

Complexity drops from O(total corpus size) to O(`parents.length`) — normally
1, since `cardParentIds()` already dedupes. Behavior is unchanged:
`parent?.status === "done"` on the `get()` result is exactly what
`cards.get(parentId)?.status === "done"` computed from the unscoped `list()`
Map for both the found and not-found (`undefined`) cases.

### Testing

- New regression test in `store.test.ts`
  (`"resolves parent dependency status with targeted lookups instead of a
  full-corpus scan"`): creates 1 parent + 8 children with `parents: [parent.id]`,
  spies on the underlying keyed store's `entries()`, completes the parent, runs
  `dispatch()`, and asserts:
  - all 8 children are promoted to `ready` (functional correctness, unchanged
    from before the fix)
  - `entries()` is called **at most once** during the dispatch pass — before
    the fix this would have been 9 calls (1 outer board-scoped `list()` + 1
    inner unscoped `list()` per parented card being checked)
- Full extension suite: **113/113 pass**
  (`npx vitest run extensions/workboard/src/`)

### Scope note

`dependsOn()` (same file) has an identical unscoped-`list()` pattern, used
only for cycle-detection at parent/child link-creation time — not on the
dispatch hot path, and there's no profiling evidence it's ever expensive in
practice (link creation is comparatively rare). Deliberately left out of this
PR to keep the change matched 1:1 to the measured problem; worth a follow-up
if it's ever shown to be hot.

### Relationship to #101895 / #84903

#101895 was our earlier report of this exact symptom (`workboard.cards.dispatch`
taking 250s+ wall-clock), which was auto-triaged as a duplicate and merged into
#84903 (generic event-loop-starvation tracker) under the theory that a
concurrent embedded/CLI agent session was starving the gateway's single event
loop. The live CPU profile above shows that, for this specific stall, that
theory doesn't hold — the cost is entirely inside `dispatch()`'s own
synchronous execution. Leaving a comment on both issues linking back to this
PR; the general event-loop-starvation question tracked in #84903 may still be
real for other symptoms, but this particular reproduction is fully explained
and fixed by the change here.

Verified locally against a real corpus (~5770 Workboard cards): the exact
`workboard.cards.dispatch` RPC call that took 160-163s wall-clock before this
fix consistently completed in **2.9s** after, with internal pass-timer
instrumentation showing the fix itself added no measurable overhead
(<1ms, consistent with pre-fix internal timings).


### Real behavior proof

Redacted excerpt from the deployed instance's own gateway log, straight from
`journalctl`, showing repeated real `workboard.cards.dispatch` RPC calls
against a live board with a ~5,770-card corpus, immediately before and after
this fix was deployed (connection/request IDs already truncated by the
logger itself; nothing else redacted):

**Before** (unscoped `list()` scan on every parented card in the pass):
```
2026-07-11T18:32:44.689Z [ws] res workboard.cards.dispatch 159519ms
2026-07-11T18:47:39.256Z [ws] res workboard.cards.dispatch 154351ms
2026-07-11T19:02:42.699Z [ws] res workboard.cards.dispatch 157688ms
2026-07-11T19:08:04.708Z [ws] res workboard.cards.dispatch 159080ms
2026-07-11T19:17:40.639Z [ws] res workboard.cards.dispatch 155731ms
2026-07-11T19:25:57.209Z [ws] res workboard.cards.dispatch 158484ms
2026-07-11T19:32:41.887Z [ws] res workboard.cards.dispatch 157259ms
```

**After** (targeted `get(parentId)` lookups; internal `pass_total`
instrumentation, unrelated to this PR, confirms the fix itself adds no
measurable overhead — consistently under 1 second before and after):
```
2026-07-11T19:43:10.772Z [ws] res workboard.cards.dispatch 2912ms
2026-07-11T19:45:07.069Z [ws] res workboard.cards.dispatch 2870ms
2026-07-11T20:00:08.020Z [ws] res workboard.cards.dispatch 2843ms
2026-07-11T20:15:07.584Z [ws] res workboard.cards.dispatch 2783ms
2026-07-11T20:30:07.233Z [ws] res workboard.cards.dispatch 2881ms
2026-07-11T20:45:07.163Z [ws] res workboard.cards.dispatch 2780ms
```

Same recurring dispatch call (a `*/15` cron against the same board/corpus),
same deployment, only the code change in between: 154-160s consistently,
every time, before; 2.7-2.9s consistently, every time, after. ~55x.

The underlying `.cpuprofile` referenced above (CDP `Profiler.start`/`stop`
captured over a live-attached inspector, 645,052 samples, 161.8s elapsed)
is not attached directly, since it's a full capture of a real, large
production Workboard corpus — chrome://inspect-format CPU profiles record
call-stack frames (function name/file/line), not card contents, but the
file/module paths and process metadata in it are unredacted and it's large
(5.4MB) enough that hand-redacting isn't practical. The self-time breakdown
already summarized above (93.3% in `all()`/`prepare()` under
`dependencyTargetStatus() -> list() -> entries() -> readCard()`) is the
finding taken directly from analyzing that profile; happy to produce a
sanitized frame-only summary if a maintainer wants to inspect it further.

## What Problem This Solves

`readParamRaw()` is a private function that directly delegates to `readSnakeCaseParamRaw()` with no additional logic. It has 7 call sites, all in the same file. Removing the wrapper and calling `readSnakeCaseParamRaw` directly eliminates unnecessary indirection.

## Real behavior proof

- **Behavior or issue addressed**: Remove unnecessary wrapper function
- **Real environment tested**: Node 22.22, Linux x86_64, local dev checkout
- **Exact steps or command run after this patch**: Exercised all 7 affected parameter readers through the actual exported API
- **Evidence after fix**:
  ```text
  $ node --import tsx -e "..."
  1. readStringParam({ str: "hello" }, "str")           → "hello"
  2. readStringParam({}, "missing")                      → undefined
  3. readStringOrNumberParam({ val: 42 }, "val")          → "42"
  4. readNumberParam({ num: 42 }, "num")                  → 42
  5. readNumberParam({ num: "3.14" }, "num")             → 3.14
  6. readNumberParam({}, "missing")                      → undefined
  7. readPositiveIntegerParam({ count: "5" }, "count")   → 5
  ```
  All 7 readers return correct values. Diff is -4 lines of dead code.
- **Observed result after fix**: Behavior unchanged; all parameter readers work identically.
- **What was not tested**: Live agent-tool invocation through a real gateway session

## Files Changed

| File | Change |
|---|---|
| `src/agents/tools/common.ts` | Removed `readParamRaw` function; call `readSnakeCaseParamRaw` directly at 7 sites |

target.title: fix(memory-core): honor private-network settings for OpenAI-compatible embeddings
target.body:
## Summary

- Rebases PR #94344 onto current main and resolves the OpenAI-compatible embedding provider conflicts without changing the intended SSRF contract.
- Updates the added SSRF tests to match the exported `LookupFn` overload shape.
- Updates the memory config docs to describe exact configured `baseUrl` origin trust (`scheme://host:port`) without widening trust across protocols or ports.
- Prevents configured local-service acquisition and health probes when the selected provider explicitly sets `request.allowPrivateNetwork: false`.
- **Why it matters / User impact:** Operators using configured OpenAI-compatible memory embedding providers need the selected provider's private-endpoint policy to behave predictably: omitted policy preserves exact configured origin compatibility, explicit `false` fails closed, and explicit `true` allows broader private-network access.
- **Scope boundary:** The rebase repair changes only the existing embedding SSRF policy integration, its tests/docs, and the local-service composition needed to honor explicit denial before any probe. It does not change schema, migrations, non-memory provider request paths, gateway/channel/session routing, global SSRF helpers, dependencies, or lockfiles.

Fixes #94166

## Origin / follow-up

N/A — existing PR author repair for #94344.

## Competition / linked PR analysis

- **Linked PR(s):** #94180 (`feat(memory-core): allow private network endpoints for memory embeddings`) and adjacent #96074 (`fix(memory): honor provider request proxy for embeddings`). The public-contract helper also flagged #92307 through an environment/version term, but #92307 is about exec-approval startup warnings and is not the same embedding/private-network contract.
- **Gap in linked PR(s):** #94180 adds a memory-specific config surface, `memorySearch.remote.network.dangerouslyAllowPrivateNetwork`, for a trust decision that the selected model provider can already express with `models.providers.<id>.request.allowPrivateNetwork`.
- **Why this patch is better/canonical:** This PR reuses the existing provider transport-trust contract as the canonical source of truth for configured providers instead of introducing a second memory-only knob. This update only repairs the review findings on that existing approach.
- **Local real behavior proof advantage:** The current-head bounded proof exercises the real `memory status --deep --json` CLI path against a loopback/private OpenAI-compatible daemon backed by the actual FastEmbed `BAAI/bge-small-en-v1.5` model. Omitted policy succeeds through exact-origin trust with one `/v1/embeddings` request, explicit `request.allowPrivateNetwork: false` is blocked before the daemon receives any request, and explicit `true` succeeds with one `/v1/embeddings` request.
- **Related open PR scan:** #94180 is the linked alternative for memory private endpoint support. #96074 is adjacent but distinct: it propagates the selected provider's proxy dispatcher into memory embedding HTTP transport, while this PR is limited to the provider's three-state private-network policy and deliberately does not pass proxy/auth/TLS fields into the policy resolver. #92307 was an environment/version false-positive and is not part of this embedding/private-network contract.

## Real behavior proof

- **Behavior or issue addressed:** `openclaw memory status --deep` against a configured OpenAI-compatible embedding endpoint on a loopback/private address must preserve exact-origin compatibility when provider private-network policy is omitted, must block when the selected provider explicitly sets `request.allowPrivateNetwork: false`, and must honor `request.allowPrivateNetwork: true` for explicit broader private-network trust.
- **Canonical reachability path:** User `models.providers.<id>` and `agents.defaults.memorySearch` config → existing config schema/type parsing and configured-provider normalization → `ConfiguredEmbeddingProvider.request.allowPrivateNetwork` on the runtime embedding client → shared SSRF policy → guarded `/v1/embeddings` request or pre-request block.
- **Boundary crossed:** Full config-to-request local runtime path through the real `openclaw memory status --deep --json` CLI and `memory-core` embedding probe into a real FastEmbed model daemon. This is local-daemon behavior proof, not third-party provider proof.
- **Shared helper / provider constraint check:** Reused the repository shared `resolveProviderTransportSsrFPolicy` policy builder and `resolvePinnedHostnameWithPolicy` test seam. This preserves the canonical exact-origin and metadata-hostname exclusions instead of rebuilding them in the embedding adapter. No numeric-string parser or provider-owned range constraint is added or changed; the only provider contract consumed is the existing boolean `request.allowPrivateNetwork` setting.
- **Real environment tested:** CLI behavior proof was captured in the local PR worktree on Linux, using the real source CLI, the real `memory-core` CLI command, isolated `OPENCLAW_CONFIG_PATH`, isolated `OPENCLAW_STATE_DIR`, isolated `OPENCLAW_HOME`, and an OpenAI-compatible FastEmbed `BAAI/bge-small-en-v1.5` daemon bound to a loopback/private address. The proof is bound to current HEAD by daily-fix's non-mock live-proof receipt. Current-head re-verification also covered the rebased runtime integration, test typing, docs wording, and the explicit-denial plus configured-local-service combination.
- **Exact steps or command run after this patch:** The live runtime proof command used for the PR behavior was:

```sh
node scripts/run-node.mjs memory status --agent proof --deep --json
```

The current rebased head was re-verified with these commands from `/media/vdb/code/ai/aispace/openclaw-worktrees/pr-94344`:

```sh
pnpm exec tsc --ignoreConfig --strict --module NodeNext --moduleResolution NodeNext --target ES2022 --types node --noEmit /media/vdb/code/ai/aispace/openclaw-pr-94344-evidence/lookupfn-overload-smoke.ts
node scripts/run-vitest.mjs run --config test/vitest/vitest.plugins.config.ts src/plugins/openai-compatible-embedding-provider.test.ts
pnpm check:test-types
git diff --check
```

- **Evidence after fix:** Exact-origin compatibility result from the real CLI, with provider `request.allowPrivateNetwork` omitted:

```json
{
  "agentId": "proof",
  "status": {
    "provider": "openai-compatible",
    "requestedProvider": "private-embedding-proof",
    "model": "BAAI/bge-small-en-v1.5"
  },
  "embeddingProbe": {
    "ok": true
  }
}
```

Exact-origin compatibility summary:

```json
{
  "code": 0,
  "containsEmbeddingsReady": true,
  "serverRequestCount": 1
}
```

Explicit provider denial result from the real CLI:

```json
{
  "agentId": "proof",
  "status": {
    "provider": "openai-compatible",
    "requestedProvider": "private-embedding-proof",
    "model": "BAAI/bge-small-en-v1.5"
  },
  "embeddingProbe": {
    "ok": false,
    "error": "Blocked hostname or private/internal/special-use IP address"
  }
}
```

Explicit provider denial summary:

```json
{
  "code": 0,
  "containsGuardBlock": true,
  "containsEmbeddingsReady": false,
  "serverRequestCount": 0
}
```

Provider opt-in overlay result from the real CLI:

```json
{
  "agentId": "proof",
  "status": {
    "provider": "openai-compatible",
    "requestedProvider": "private-embedding-proof",
    "model": "BAAI/bge-small-en-v1.5"
  },
  "embeddingProbe": {
    "ok": true
  }
}
```

Provider opt-in overlay summary:

